paragraphs.text: In my view, the strongest case for protecting uninterrupted study time rests on what we actually know about how the brain handles demanding work.

Sustained attention to complex material relies on a fragile state of cognitive engagement that, once disrupted, cannot be resumed instantaneously; empirical studies of knowledge workers indicate that recovery from a single interruption can require upwards of twenty minutes before full task immersion is reestablished.

Furthermore, the phenomenon known as attention residue describes the lingering preoccupation with a prior task that continues to occupy working memory even after attention has nominally shifted, thereby degrading performance on the subsequent activity and compounding the cost of each successive disruption.
This matters most for the kind of deep, integrative thinking that college work demands.

The deliberate practice required to master genuinely difficult cognitive skills depends upon extended, distraction-free intervals in which the learner can hold multiple variables in mind simultaneously and forge the durable neural connections that constitute true expertise.

By contrast, environments characterized by frequent context-switching have been shown to elevate cortisol levels, diminish working-memory capacity, and produce a measurable decline in the quality of analytical reasoning, with the most pronounced deficits appearing precisely in tasks that require novel problem-solving rather than rote recall.

Taken together, that evidence makes the defense of protected study time less a matter of student preference and more a question of designing campuses around the conditions under which real learning is even possible.
